hero.description: Global hepatitis B prevalence, chronic infection rates, cirrhosis and liver cancer deaths, birth-dose vaccination coverage, and elimination targets toward 2030.

trends.note: Vaccine introduction has driven a sustained decline in new infections since the 1990s, particularly among children.

riskFactors.title: Mother-to-Child Transmission
riskFactors.description: Perinatal transmission from HBV-infected mothers is the most common route in high-prevalence regions. Without intervention, up to 90% of infected newborns develop chronic infection.

riskFactors.title: Unsafe Injections & Blood Exposure
riskFactors.description: Reuse of needles in healthcare settings and unscreened blood transfusions remain major transmission routes in low-income countries.

riskFactors.title: Unscreened Blood & Organs
riskFactors.description: In regions without universal blood screening, transfusions and organ transplants carry significant HBV transmission risk.

riskFactors.title: Sexual Transmission
riskFactors.description: HBV is 50–100 times more infectious than HIV through sexual contact. Unprotected sex with infected partners is a significant route in low-prevalence regions.

riskFactors.title: Low Diagnosis & Treatment Awareness
riskFactors.description: Only 13% of the 254 million people with chronic HBV know their status. Hepatitis B is largely asymptomatic, enabling silent progression to cirrhosis and liver cancer.

didYouKnow: Hepatitis B is 50–100 times more infectious than HIV and can survive outside the body for up to 7 days.
The hepatitis B vaccine is one of medicine's greatest success stories — it has prevented an estimated 1 billion infections since introduction.
Chronic HBV is the leading cause of liver cancer globally, responsible for approximately 50% of all hepatocellular carcinoma cases.
Only 3% of the 254 million people who need hepatitis B treatment are actually receiving it worldwide.

faq.a: Chronic hepatitis B is not curable with current treatments, but it is manageable. Antiviral medications (tenofovir, entecavir) can suppress viral replication to very low levels, preventing liver damage, cirrhosis, and liver cancer. Acute hepatitis B resolves on its own in about 95% of adults.

faq.q: Is there a vaccine for hepatitis B?
faq.a: Yes. A safe, effective 3-dose vaccine has been available since 1982. WHO recommends universal infant vaccination with a birth dose within 24 hours. The vaccine is 95% effective at preventing infection and its chronic consequences.

faq.q: What is the WHO 2030 elimination target for hepatitis B?
faq.a: WHO's global health sector strategy targets a 90% reduction in new chronic HBV infections and a 65% reduction in hepatitis B mortality by 2030. Achieving this requires 90% birth-dose vaccination coverage, 90% childhood vaccination, and 80% treatment coverage.
